title: Letters to Atticus
author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
source: Translated by Claude from phi0474.phi057.perseus-lat1, as held by the Perseus Digital Library.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: nam Catonem nostrum non tu amas plus quam ego; sed tamen ille optimo animo utens et summa fide nocet interdum rei publicae; dicit enim tamquam in Platonis πολιτείᾳ, non tamquam in Romuli faece sententiam. quid verius quam in iudicium venire qui ob rem iudicandam pecuniam acceperit? censuit hoc Cato, adsensit senatus; equites curiae bellum, non mihi;
passages.english: For you do not love our Cato more than I do; but all the same, though he acts with the best intentions and the greatest integrity, he sometimes harms the republic; for he speaks his opinion as though he were in Plato's Republic, not in the dregs of Romulus. What is more just than that a man who has taken money for judging a case should be brought to trial? Cato proposed this, the senate agreed; the equestrians [declared] war on the senate house, not on me;

passages.original: atque haec sic velim existimes non me abs te κατὰ τὸ πρακτικὸν quaerere, quod gestiat animus aliquid agere in re publica. iam pridem gubernare me taedebat, etiam cum licebat; nunc vero cum cogar exire de navi non abiectis sed ereptis gubernaculis, cupio istorum naufragia ex terra intueri, cupio, ut ait tuus amicus Sophocles, κἂν ὑπὸ στέγῃ πυκνῆσ ἀκούειν ψακάδοσ εὑδούσῃ φρενί.
passages.english: And I would like you to understand that I am not asking you these things with a practical purpose, because my mind is eager to do something in public affairs. For a long time now I have been weary of steering, even when I was allowed to; but now, when I am forced to leave the ship, with the rudder not thrown away but wrenched from me, I long to watch those men's shipwrecks from the land; I long, as your friend Sophocles says, "even under a roof to hear the thick-falling rain with a sleeping mind."
passages.notes: The Greek quotation is from a lost play of Sophocles; text slightly garbled in the scan (πυκνῆσ, ψακάδοσ for πυκνῆς, ψακάδος).

passages.original: ut in oratoriis, quos tu in caelum fers, non potuit mentio fieri cuiusquam ab iis qui disputant, nisi eius qui illis notus aut auditus esset, ita hanc ego de re publica quam institui disputationem in Africani personam et Phili et Laeli et Manili contuli. adiunxi adulescentis Q. Tuberonem, P. Rutilium, duo Laeli generos, Scaevolam et Fannium. itaque cogitabam, quoniam in singulis libris utor prohoemiis ut Aristoteles in iis quos ἐξωτερικοὺσ vocat, aliquid efficere ut non sine causa istum appellarem; id quod intellego tibi placere. utinam modo conata efficere possim! rem enim, quod te non fugit, magnam complexus sum et gravem et plurimi oti, quo ego maxime egeo.
passages.english: Just as in the dialogues on oratory, which you praise to the skies, no mention could be made by the speakers of anyone except someone they had known or heard, so I have assigned this discussion on the republic that I have begun to the persons of Africanus, Philus, Laelius and Manilius. I have added the young men Quintus Tubero and Publius Rutilius, and Laelius' two sons-in-law, Scaevola and Fannius. So I was thinking, since in each book I use prefaces, as Aristotle does in those works he calls "exoteric," of contriving something so that I could name that man [Varro] with good reason; which I understand you would like. If only I can accomplish what I have attempted! For I have taken on, as you are well aware, a great and weighty task, one requiring a great deal of leisure, which is what I most lack.

passages.original: iiii Non. Novembr. triumphare. huic obviam Cato et Servilius praetores ad portam et Q. Mucius tribunus. negant enim latum de imperio, et est latum hercule insulse. sed erit cum Pomptino Appius consul. Cato tamen adfirmat se vivo illum non triumphaturum. id ego puto ut multa eiusdem ad nihilum recasurum. Appius sine lege suo sumptu in Ciliciam cogitat.
passages.english: [Pomptinus wants] to triumph on the fourth day before the Nones of November. The praetors Cato and Servilius and the tribune Quintus Mucius [will] meet him at the gate. For they say no law was passed about his command, and indeed, by Hercules, it was passed clumsily. But Appius the consul will be on Pomptinus' side. Cato, however, asserts that while he lives that man will not triumph. I think that, like many of his [declarations], this will come to nothing. Appius is planning [to go] to Cilicia without a law, at his own expense.
passages.notes: Sentence begins mid-construction; 'Pomptinus vult a. d.' from the preceding context supplies the subject. 'Meet him' verb implied.

passages.original: Cicerones pueri amant inter se, exercentur, sed discunt, alter, uti dixit Isocrates in Ephoro et Theopompo, frenis eget, alter calcaribus. Quinto togam puram Liberalibus cogitabam dare; mandavit enim pater. ea sic observabo quasi intercalatum non sit. Dionysius mihi quidem in amoribus est; pueri autem aiunt eum furenter irasci;
passages.english: The boys, the two Ciceros, love each other, they are being trained, they are learning; but, as Isocrates said of Ephorus and Theopompus, one needs the reins, the other the spurs. I was thinking of giving Quintus the plain toga at the Liberalia; for his father asked me to. I shall observe that date as though there had been no intercalation. Dionysius is certainly a favourite of mine; but the boys say that he gets furiously angry;
passages.notes: "The Ciceros" are Cicero's son Marcus and his nephew Quintus. The "plain toga" (toga pura) is the toga of manhood. The Liberalia fell on 17 March.

passages.original: o ἀνιστορησίαν turpem! nam illud de Flavio et fastis, si secus est, commune erratum est et tu belle ἠπόρησασ et nos publicam prope opinionem secuti sumus, ut multa apud Graecos. quis enim non dixit Εὔπολιν τὸν τῆσ ἀρχαίασ ab Alcibiade navigante in Siciliam deiectum esse in mare? redarguit Eratosthenes; adfert enim quas ille post id tempus fabulas docuerit. num idcirco Duris Samius, homo in historia diligens, quod cum multis erravit, inridetur?
passages.english: O shameful ignorance of history! For as to that point about Flavius and the calendar, if it is otherwise, the error is a common one. You were right to raise the doubt, and I followed what is almost the general opinion, as happens with many things among the Greeks. For who has not said that Eupolis, the poet of Old Comedy, was thrown into the sea by Alcibiades as he was sailing to Sicily? Eratosthenes refutes it, for he cites plays that Eupolis produced after that time. Is Duris of Samos, a careful man in history, laughed at on that account, because he erred along with many others?
passages.notes: Greek in the original: ἀνιστορησίαν ("ignorance of history"), ἠπόρησας ("you raised a doubt"), Εὔπολιν τὸν τῆς ἀρχαίας ("Eupolis of the Old [Comedy]"). The reading "ἠπόρησασ" is taken as ἠπόρησας. "Fasti" here refers to the calendar of court days.

passages.original: illum autem multa de istis rebus asperius solete loqui saepe sum expertus, saepe etiam lenivi iratum. id scire te arbitror. in hac autem peregrinatione militiave nostra saepe incensum ira vidi, saepe placatum. quid ad Statium scripserit nescio. quicquid acturus de tali re fuit, scribendum tamen ad libertum non fuit. mihi autem erit maximae curae ne quid fiat secus quam volumus quamque oportet. nec satis est in eius modi re se quemque praestare ac maximae partes istius offici sunt pueri Ciceronis sive iam adulescentis;
passages.english: I have often found that he is accustomed to speak rather harshly about those matters, and often too I have calmed him when angry. I think you know this. But in this travelling or campaigning of ours I have often seen him inflamed with anger, often appeased. What he wrote to Statius I do not know. Whatever he was going to do about such a matter, he still should not have written to a freedman. But it will be my greatest concern that nothing happens otherwise than we wish and than is proper. Nor is it enough in a matter of this kind for each to answer for himself, and the greatest part of that duty belongs to the boy Cicero, or rather by now young man;

passages.original: haec a me ordine facta puto me Bruto probaturum, tibi nescio, Catoni certe probabo. sed iam ad te ipsum revertor. ain tandem, Attice, laudator integritatis et elegantiae nostrae, ausus es hoc ex ore tuo— — inquit Ennius, ut equites Scaptio ad pecuniam cogendam darem me rogare? an tu si mecum esses qui scribis morderi te interdum quod non simul sis, paterere me id facere si vellem? non amplius inquis quinquaginta.cum Spartaco minus multi primo fuerunt.
passages.english: I think I shall get Brutus to approve these things that I did in proper order. You, I don't know; Cato I certainly shall. But now I return to you yourself. Do you really say so, Atticus, you who praise my integrity and good taste? "Did you dare [to let] this [pass] from your mouth," as Ennius says, to ask me to give Scaptius cavalry for collecting his money? If you were with me, you who write that you are sometimes stung that you are not with me, would you allow me to do it, even if I wished? "No more than fifty," you say. There were fewer with Spartacus at first.
passages.notes: The Ennius quotation is incomplete in the text (marked by dashes); the bracketed words are supplied. The reading "quinquaginta.cum" is taken as two sentences.

passages.original: Coelio quaestori relinquere annuum, referre in aerarium ad HS †cIↃ†, ingemuit nostra cohors omne illud putans distribui sibi oportere, ut ego amicior invenirer Phrygum et Cilicum aerariis quam nostro. sed me non moverunt; nam et mea laus apud me plurimum valuit nec tamen quicquam honorifice in quemquam fieri potuit quod praetermiserim. sed haec fuerit ut ait Thucydides, ἐκβολὴ λόγου non inutilis.
passages.english: [I thought it right] to leave a year's allowance to the quaestor Gaius Coelius and to return to the treasury about †...† sesterces; my staff groaned, thinking all that ought to be distributed to them, so that I would be found more friendly to the treasuries of the Phrygians and Cilicians than to our own. But they did not move me; for both my own good name weighed most with me, and yet nothing could be done honourably for anyone that I left undone. But let this have been, as Thucydides says, a not unprofitable digression.
passages.notes: The sum is corrupt in the text (†cIↃ†, perhaps 1,000 or a larger figure); not translated. 'C.' from context = Gaius.

passages.original: ei porro adsensus est unus familiaris meus, Favonius, alter iratus, Hirrus. Cato autem et scribendo adfuit et ad me de sententia sua iucundissimas litteras misit. sed tamen gratulans mihi Caesar de supplicatione triumphat de sententia Catonis nec scribit quid ille sententiae dixerit sed tantum supplicationem eum mihi non decrevisse.
passages.english: He was further supported by two men: one my friend, Favonius, the other angry [with me], Hirrus. Cato, however, was both present at the drafting [of the decree] and sent me a most pleasant letter about his opinion. Yet Caesar, congratulating me on the thanksgiving, exults over Cato's vote, and does not write what opinion he expressed, but only that he did not vote me a thanksgiving.

passages.original: nihil ei me gratius facere posse. haec verbis plurimis. intellexi ex dierum ratione, ut primum de discessu nostro Caesar audisset, laborare eum coepisse ne omnes abessemus. itaque non dubito quin ad Pisonem, quin ad Servium scripserit; illud admiror non ipsum ad me scripsisse, non per Dolabellam, non per Caelium egisse. quamquam non aspernor Trebati litteras, a quo me unice diligi scio.
passages.english: [and that] I could do nothing more pleasing to him. This [was said] at great length. I gathered from the reckoning of the dates that as soon as Caesar had heard of our departure he began to be anxious that we should not all be absent. So I do not doubt that he has written to Piso and to Servius; what surprises me is that he has not written to me himself, nor dealt [with me] through Dolabella or through Caelius. Still, I do not despise the letter of Trebatius, by whom I know I am loved exceptionally.

passages.original: beneficia eiusdem cogito, cogito etiam dignitatem; intellego serius equidem quam vellem propter epistulas sermonesque Balbi, sed video plane nihil aliud agi, nihil actum ab initio, nisi ut hunc occideret. ego igitur, sicut ille apud Homerum cui et mater et dea dixisset, αὐτίκα γάρ τοι ἔπειτα μεθ' Ἕκτορα πότμοσ ἕτοιμος, matri ipse respondit, αὐτίκα τεθναίην, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἄρ' ἔμελλον ἑταίρῳ κτεινομένῳ ἐπαμῦναι, quid si non ἑταίρῳ solum sed etiam εὐεργέτῃ, adde tali viro talem causam agenti? ego vero haec officia mercanda vita puto.
passages.english: I think of his favours, I think too of his standing; I understand, later indeed than I would have wished, because of Balbus' letters and conversations, but I see plainly that nothing else is being aimed at, nothing has been aimed at from the beginning, except that he should kill this man. So I, like that man in Homer to whom his mother, a goddess too, had said, "For straightaway after Hector your doom is ready," and who himself answered his mother, "May I die straightaway, since I was not to help my comrade when he was slain" — what if [it is] not only a comrade but also a benefactor, and add, such a man pleading such a cause? I truly think such duties are to be bought with one's life.

passages.original: Caesar mihi ignoscit per litteras quod non venerim, seseque in optimam partem id accipere dicit. facile patior, quod scribit, secum Titinium et Servium questos esse quia non idem sibi quod mihi remisisset. homines ridiculos! qui cum filios misissent ad Cn. Pompeium circumsedendum, ipsi in senatum venire dubitarint. sed tamen exemplum misi ad te Caesaris litterarum.
passages.english: Caesar forgives me by letter for not having come, and says he takes it in the best part. I bear it easily when he writes that Titinius and Servius complained to him because he had not granted them the same indulgence as me. Ridiculous men! They sent their sons to besiege Gnaeus Pompeius, and yet they themselves hesitated to come to the senate. But anyway, I have sent you a copy of Caesar's letter.

passages.original: quod si me fefellerit, feram, sicut multi clarissimi homines in re publica excellentes tulerunt, nisi forte me Sardanapalli vicem in suo lectulo mori malle censueris quam in exsilio Themistocleo. qui cum fuisset, ut ait Thucydides, τῶν μὲν παρόντων δι', tamen incidit in eos casus quos vitasset si eum nihil fefellisset. etsi is erat ut ait idem, qui τὸ ἄμεινον καὶ τὸ χεῖρον ἐν τῷ ἀφανεῖ ἔτι ἑώρα μάλιστα, tamen non vidit nec quo modo Lacedaemoniorum nec quo modo suorum civium invidiam effugeret nec quid Artaxerxi polliceretur.
passages.english: But if it deceives me, I will bear it, as many most distinguished men eminent in the state have borne it, unless perhaps you think I should prefer to die in my bed like Sardanapallus rather than in exile like Themistocles. Though he was, as Thucydides says, [the best judge] of present matters, yet he fell into misfortunes he would have avoided if nothing had deceived him. Although he was, as the same author says, one who most of all foresaw the better and the worse while still hidden, yet he did not see either how to escape the hatred of the Lacedaemonians or of his own citizens, or what to promise Artaxerxes.
passages.notes: The Thucydides quotation is truncated in the text (τῶν μὲν παρόντων δι'...); sense supplied in brackets.

passages.original: tutius videbatur fore ibi ubi est quam apud publicanos. quod me hortaris ut firmo sim animo, vellem posses aliquid adferre quam ob rem id facere possem. sed si ad ceteras miserias accessit etiam id quod mihi Chrysippus dixit parari (tu nihil significasti) de domo, quis me miserior uno iam fuit? oro, obsecro, ignosce. non possum plura scribere. quanto maerore urgear profecto vides. quod si mihi commune cum ceteris esset qui videntur in eadem causa esse, minor mea culpa videretur et eo tolerabilior esset.
passages.english: It seemed it would be safer where it is than with the tax-farmers. As for your urging me to be steadfast in spirit, I wish you could offer some reason why I could do so. But if, on top of my other miseries, there has come also what Chrysippus told me was being prepared regarding my house (you gave no hint of it), who has ever been more wretched than I alone? I beg, I implore you, forgive me. I cannot write more. You surely see how great a grief weighs on me. But if my situation were shared with the others who seem to be in the same position, my fault would seem less and so more bearable.
passages.notes: Subject of the first sentence (probably money) is not stated in the passage.

passages.original: de Caelio vide, quaeso, ne quae lacuna sit in auro. ego ista non novi. sed certe in collubo est detrimenti satis. huc aurum si accedit—sed quid loquor? tu videbis. habes Hegesiae genus, quod Varro laudat.
passages.english: About Caelius, please see that there is no deficiency in the gold. I do not know about these things. But certainly there is enough loss in the exchange charge. If the gold is added to this... but what am I saying? You will see to it. There you have the Hegesias style, which Varro praises.
passages.notes: "Collubus" (usually collybus) is the agio, the fee for exchanging money. Hegesias was an Asianic orator known for a choppy style.

passages.original: legi Bruti epistulam eamque tibi remisi sane non prudenter rescriptum ad ea quae requisieras. sed ipse viderit. quamquam illud turpiter ignorat. Catonem primum sententiam putat de animadversione dixisse quam omnes ante dixerant praeter Caesarem et, cum ipsius Caesaris tam severa fuerit qui tum praetorio loco dixerit, consularium putat leniores fuisse, Catuli, Servili, Lucullorum, Curionis, Torquati, Lepidi, Gelli, Volcaci, Figuli, Cottae, L.
passages.english: I have read Brutus' letter and sent it back to you; the reply to the points you had raised was certainly not well judged. But that is his own affair. And yet he is shamefully ignorant on one point. He thinks Cato was the first to state the motion for punishment, when everyone before him had stated it except Caesar; and although Caesar's own [motion], he who then spoke among the praetorians, was so severe, he thinks those of the consulars were milder: Catulus, Servilius, the Luculli, Curio, Torquatus, Lepidus, Gellius, Volcacius, Figulus, Cotta, L.
passages.notes: Refers to the senate debate of 5 December 63 BC on the Catilinarian conspirators. The list continues in the following passage (L. Caesar).

passages.original: Hirti epistulam si legeris, quae mihi quasi πρόπλασμα videtur eius vituperationis quam Caesar scripsit de Catone, facies me quid tibi visum sit, si tibi erit commodum, certiorem. redeo ad fanum. nisi hac aestate absolutum erit quam vides integram restare, scelere me liberatum non putabo.
passages.english: If you read Hirtius' letter, which seems to me a sort of *proplasma* (preliminary sketch) of the invective that Caesar has written about Cato, please let me know, if it is convenient for you, what you thought of it. I return to the shrine. Unless it is finished this summer, which, as you see, remains wholly ahead of us, I shall not consider myself freed from guilt.
passages.notes: The 'shrine' (fanum) is the memorial Cicero planned for his daughter Tullia. 'Scelere' (guilt, crime) is strong: he would feel guilty of a wrong toward her.

passages.original: quod ad me de Varrone scribis, scis me antea orationes aut aliquid id genus solitum scribere ut Varronem nusquam possem intexere. postea autem quam haec coepi φιλολογώτερα, iam Varro mihi denuntiaverat magnam sane et gravem προσφώνησιν. biennium praeteriit cum ille Καλλιπίδησ adsiduo cursu cubitum nullum processerit, ego autem me parabam ad id quod ille mihi misisset ut αὐτῷ τῷ μέτρῳ καὶ, si modo potuissem;
passages.english: As to what you write to me about Varro: you know that before, I used to write speeches or something of that kind, so that I could nowhere work Varro in. But after I began these more scholarly works, Varro had already announced to me a dedication, a large and weighty one indeed. Two years have passed while he, like Callippides, running continuously, has not advanced a cubit. I, on my part, was preparing to repay what he would send me "with the same measure and [better]," if only I could;
passages.notes: Greek: φιλολογώτερα ("more scholarly"), προσφώνησιν ("dedication"), Καλλιπίδης (Callippides, proverbially one who runs without getting anywhere), αὐτῷ τῷ μέτρῳ καὶ ("with the same measure and", from Hesiod; the quotation breaks off, and "[better]" is supplied from the Hesiodic line).

passages.original: non enim sustinent sed alio modo remigant. id ab ἐποχῇ remotissimum est. qua re facies ut ita sit in libro quem ad modum fuit. dices hoc idem Varroni, si forte mutavit. nec est melius quicquam quam ut Lucilius, sustineas currum ut bonus saepe agitator equosque.semperque Carneades προβολὴν pugilis et retentionem aurigae similem facit ἐποχῇ. inhibitio autem remigum motum habet et vehementiorem quidem remigationis navem convertentis ad puppim.
passages.english: For they do not hold [the oars] but row in another way. That is very far from epochē [suspension of judgement]. So please make sure it stands in the book as it was. Tell Varro the same, if he happens to have changed it. Nor is there anything better than [to act] as Lucilius [says]: "that you hold back the chariot and horses, as a good driver often does." And Carneades always likens epochē to a boxer's guard and a charioteer's checking [of his horses]. But the inhibitio of rowers involves motion, and indeed a rather violent rowing motion, one that turns the ship round towards the stern.
passages.notes: Greek: ἐποχή (epochē, suspension of judgement), προβολήν (a boxer's guard). The discussion concerns whether the Latin verb "inhibere" (to back water) is a fit rendering for epochē.

passages.original: hanc autem causam pater odium matris esse dicebat. nunc me iuva, mi Attice, consilio, πότερον id est utrum aperte hominem asperner et respuam, ἢ σκολιαῖσ ἀπάταις. ut enim Pindaro sic δίχα μοι νόοσ ἀτρέκειαν εἰπεῖν.omnino moribus meis illud aptius sed hoc fortasse temporibus. tu autem quod ipse tibi suaseris idem mihi persuasum putato. equidem vereor maxime ne in Tusculano opprimar.
passages.english: The cause of this, his father said, was hatred of his mother. Now help me with advice, my dear Atticus: *poteron*, that is, whether I should openly spurn and reject the man, 'or by crooked deceits'. For, as with Pindar, 'my mind is divided in telling the truth'. The former is altogether more suited to my character, but the latter perhaps to the times. As for you, consider that whatever you persuade yourself of, I am persuaded of the same. For my part, I am most afraid of being caught off guard at my Tusculan villa.
passages.notes: Greek phrases from a Pindar fragment. 'The man' is probably the younger Quintus Cicero, but the referent is not explicit in the passage.

passages.original: Balbum conveni—Lepta enim de sua munerum curatione laborans me ad eum perduxerat—in eo autem Lanuvino quod Lepido tradidit. ex eo hoc primum, Paulo ante acceperam eas litteras in quibus magno opere confirmat ante ludos Romanos.legi epistulam. multa de meo Catone, quo saepissime legendo se dicit copiosiorem factum, Bruti Catone lecto se sibi visum disertum.
passages.english: I met Balbus (for Lepta, worried about his commission for the games, had taken me to him) at that Lanuvian villa which he has handed over to Lepidus. From him [I heard] this first: 'A little earlier I had received that letter in which he strongly affirms [that he will come] before the Roman Games.' I read the letter. [There was] much about my *Cato*: by reading it very often he says he has become more fluent, but after reading Brutus' *Cato* he thought himself eloquent.
passages.notes: The text seems defective around 'ante ludos Romanos'; something like 'he will come' must be supplied. 'He' in the letter is presumably Caesar. The final contrast is uncertain; the sense may be that Brutus' Cato made him think himself eloquent by comparison.

passages.original: Statius scripsit ad me locutum secum esse Q. Ciceronem valde adseveranter se haec ferre non posse; certum sibi esse ad Brutum et Cassium transire. hoc enim vero nunc discere aveo, hoc ego quid sit interpretari non possum.
passages.english: Statius has written to me that Quintus Cicero [the younger] told him very emphatically that he could not bear these things; that he was determined to go over to Brutus and Cassius. This, indeed, I am now eager to learn: what this means I cannot interpret.

passages.original: recusasse autem se ne patris animum offenderet; ex eo sibi illum hostem. tum me inquit conlegi verens ne quid mihi ille iratus tibi noceret. itaque eum placavi. et quidem c_c_c_c_ certa, reliqua in spe.scribit autem Statius illum cum patre habitare velle (hoc vero mirum) et id gaudet. ecquem tu illo certiorem nebulonem?
passages.english: [He wrote that] he had refused so as not to offend his father's feelings, and that because of this [Antonius] had become his enemy. 'Then', he says, 'I pulled myself together, fearing that in his anger he might do some harm to you. So I appeased him. And in fact [I have] [...] certain, the rest in prospect.' Statius writes, moreover, that he wants to live with his father (this is astonishing indeed), and [his father] is delighted. Do you know any more thoroughgoing rascal than him?
passages.notes: 'c_c_c_c_' is corrupt; probably a sum of money (e.g. 400,000 sesterces) has been lost. 'certiorem nebulonem' is rendered 'more thoroughgoing rascal'.

passages.original: quod vereris ne ἀδόλεσχοσ mihi tu, quis minus? cui, ut Aristophani Archilochi iambus, sic epistula tua longissima quaeque optima videtur. quod me admones, tu vero etiam si reprenderes, non modo facile paterer sed etiam laetarer, quippe cum in reprensione sit prudentia cum εὐμενείᾳ.
passages.english: As for your fear that you are a chatterer to me: who less? To me, as each iambus of Archilochus seemed to Aristophanes, so each of your letters seems the best when it is the longest. As for your advising me: indeed, even if you were to find fault with me, I should not only bear it easily but even be glad, since in your criticism there is good sense together with goodwill.
passages.notes: Greek: ἀδόλεσχος ("chatterer"), εὐμενείᾳ ("goodwill"). The Aristophanes meant is probably the grammarian Aristophanes of Byzantium.
